parts:
Dear members of the lavaan group,


I am currently working on a growth curve model for fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) in breast cancer survivers who followed an online therapy.
I am having trouble defining the difference between groups (i.e. intervention versus controls) with the growth() function. My apologies in advance, this will be a long post as I aim to be as complete as possible.

The model is as follows:

model3<- '

i =~ 1*T0_FCRI_S + 1*T1_FCRI_S + 1*T2_FCRI_S #intercept with fixed coefficients
s =~ 0*T0_FCRI_S + 1*T1_FCRI_S + 2*T2_FCRI_S         #slope with fixed coefficients

#regressions
i ~ Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ T0_treatment_chemo_01+ T0_revalidatie_01+ 
    T0_psych_01 + T0_selfm_alg + T0_selfm_coping + T0_selfm_selfhelp + T0_FCRI_CS

s ~ Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ T0_treatment_chemo_01+ T0_revalidatie_01+ 
    T0_psych_01 + T0_selfm_alg + T0_selfm_coping + T0_selfm_selfhelp + T0_FCRI_CS

#time-varying covariates
T0_FCRI_S ~ T0_PDQ_PH + T0_PDQ_AT + T0_PDQ_DE + T0_PDQ_SP
T1_FCRI_S ~ T1_PDQ_PH + T1_PDQ_AT + T1_PDQ_DE + T1_PDQ_SP
T2_FCRI_S ~ T2_PDQ_PH + T2_PDQ_AT + T2_PDQ_DE + T2_PDQ_SP
'

fit3<- growth (model3, data = df, estimator = 'MLR', missing = 'ML', group = 'Randomisation')

As you can see in the model, there are many predictors (age, education, the kind of treatment they received, etc.) that we hypothesize to have an influence on the effects of this training (i.e. an hypothesized decrease in fear of cancer recurrence (FCRI_S) after the therapy).
The main question is, however, whether the groups (Randomisation = intervention versus control) differ in their decrease of FCR.

messages.subject: Re: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
parts: but this is not the effect that I am looking for (?) (i.e. whether there is an overall difference in slope), since I am interested in the difference of the slope between groups.

What about the slope?  The average slope?  The syntax that constraints the slope (co)variances to zero posits that individuals (within both groups) have identical trajectories.  If you want to compare the average slope across groups, you need to constrain that parameter to equality

s ~ c(a1, a1)*1

1. Is there a way of constraining the slopes per group with the growth() function?
(do I use 'group =' or not?)

If you want to compare groups, you need the group= argument.  Are you asking about the group.equal= argument?  Specifying group.equal = "means" would constrain all latent means to equality across groups, which is not what you want.  Use the syntax I showed above.
3. Is this approach also applicable when investigating the full model including the predictors?

If you have predictors of the slope, then you are comparing intercepts across groups.  Thus, the test would be conditional on how your predictors are centered.  This is the same as the homogeneity of slopes assumption when comparing "adjusted means" in ANCOVA (equivalent to comparing intercepts).  To make an unconditional test of equality of intercepts, the effects of predictors on the latent growth factors would have to be constrained to equality across groups.  You should test that set of constraints first, to make sure it holds.  If it does not, then that implies an interaction between the predictor(s) and the Randomization variable.  In which case you could probe the interaction by centering the predictors at 2 or 3 meaningful values, and testing equivalence of intercepts at each of those values.

http://quantpsy.org/interact/lca2.htm

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

parts: would you suggest to use group.equal = c("regressions")? Or do it individually:
I would specify constraints explicitly in the model syntax, so you know exactly what you are doing.

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ c(a1,a1)*T0_educ + c(a1,a1)*Home_alone+ c(a1,a1)*Home_child+c(a1,a1)* T0_treatment_chemo_01+ c(a1,a1)*T0_revalidatie_01+
   c(a1,a1)*T0_psych_01 + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_alg + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_coping + c(a1,a1)*T0_selfm_selfhelp
'

This constrains all variables to have the same effect, which is not what you want to do.  You just want each variable's effect to be the same in both groups.

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ c(b1,b1)*T0_educ + c(c1,c1)*Home_alone+ ...
(can I also just use 's ~ c(a1, a1)*1' here?)

Again, don't use the same label to constrain intercepts across groups that you use to constrain other parameters across groups, because any parameter with the same label will be forced to have the same value.

But don't make this constraint yet.  First compare the unrestricted model (ModUN: no constraints across groups) to the model with constrained effects on the latent slope (ModHomog).  

IFF (if and only if) that model comparison is not significant (refer to the anova() output), then compare ModHomog to a model with the same constraints but additionally constraints the intercepts across groups.  That second model-comparison will tell you whether the average slope significantly differs across groups, controlling for age, educ, etc.

- individually -

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ T0_treatment_chemo_01+ T0_revalidatie_01+ 
   T0_psych_01 + T0_selfm_alg + T0_selfm_coping + T0_selfm_selfhelp
With the latter I could test for each predictor whether there is an interaction with Randomization, which can be followed up with the steps you described.

Yes, that is correct.  But I would start with an omnibus test of whether all effects on the latent slope can be constrained across groups.  IFF that is significant, then at least one effect differs across groups, and you can conduct these individual tests as post-hoc comparisons to see which interactions need to be probed instead of making a single comparison of the intercept across groups, as described above.

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ c(b1,b1)*T0_educ + c(c1,c1)*Home_alone+ ...

(can I also just use 's ~ c(a1, a1)*1' here?)

Again, don't use the same label to constrain intercepts across groups that you use to constrain other parameters across groups, because any parameter with the same label will be forced to have the same value.

But don't make this constraint yet.  First compare the unrestricted model (ModUN: no constraints across groups) to the model with constrained effects on the latent slope (ModHomog).  

IFF (if and only if) that model comparison is not significant (refer to the anova() output), then compare ModHomog to a model with the same constraints but additionally constraints the intercepts across groups.  That second model-comparison will tell you whether the average slope significantly differs across groups, controlling for age, educ, etc.

- individually -

s ~ c(a1,a1)*Age+ T0_educ + Home_alone+ Home_child+ T0_treatment_chemo_01+ T0_revalidatie_01+ 
   T0_psych_01 + T0_selfm_alg + T0_selfm_coping + T0_selfm_selfhelp

With the latter I could test for each predictor whether there is an interaction with Randomization, which can be followed up with the steps you described.

Yes, that is correct.  But I would start with an omnibus test of whether all effects on the latent slope can be constrained across groups.  IFF that is significant, then at least one effect differs across groups, and you can conduct these individual tests as post-hoc comparisons to see which interactions need to be probed instead of making a single comparison of the intercept across groups, as described above.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: growth() model with two groups: equality constraints and 'group = '
parts: The conclusion so far is that there is no difference between average slope. On the other hand, ModUn and ModHomog do not differ significantly

I'm confused by your use of "on the other hand," which suggests you might be testing constraints in the wrong order.  First, compare ModUn and ModHomog.  Because that test is not significant, you can't reject the null hypothesis that the effects of covariates on the latent slope do not differ across groups.  In other words, the effect of a covariate on the slope (i.e., the 2-way interaction between Time and the covariate) does not depend on Group (i.e., there is no evidence of a 3-way interaction between Group, Time, and a covariate).

Then, you can validly constrain the mean of the latent slope to test whether the effect of time differs across groups (i.e., is there a Time by Group 2-way interaction), controlling for those covariates.  Sounds like you can't reject the null on that one either.
but ModHomog differs from the model that restricts both latent intercept and slope.

Please refer to parameters, not variables, as being constrained.  OK, so if you only constrain the latent slope's mean (I assume), the test is not significant.  But if you constrain the mean of both the latent intercept and the latent slope, then the test is significant?  That is a simultaneous of 2 different 2-way interactions.  You don't need to test those at the same time.  You tested the latent slope's mean and found not evidence of a group mean-difference above, so leave that constraint in place.

If you also want to test whether the mean of the latent intercept differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a significant "main" effect of Group on the outcome at Time 0), you first need to establish whether the effect of covariate(s) on the latent intercepts differs across groups (i.e., whether there is a covariate by Group 2-way interaction).  To do so, you can continue to use the model in which the latent slope's mean was constrained across groups (since you failed to reject that null hypothesis) as the baseline model (i.e., the new "unconstrained model" for the next test).  Compare that model to a model in which the effect of each covariate on the latent intercept is equal across groups (just like you did for effects on the latent slope).  If that constraint holds, you can then additionally constrain the mean of the latent intercept to equality across groups to see if fit gets worse (which would indicate a significant main effect of Group).
However, when conducting follow-up test on the models with single restrictions on parameters one by one, no parameter-slope effect seems to differ between groups.

It is unclear which parameters you are talking about, so please be explicit.  Do you mean that you tested the effect of one covariate at a time of the latent intercept, and you didn't find a single significant group difference?  Even though the omnibus simultaneous test of all covariates' effects on the latent intercept was significant?  Well, I suppose many small differences could add up to a big enough discrepancy in the omnibus test.  But I think it is not easy to explain why this occurs because your covariates are probably correlated.  Therefore, their effects are also correlated, so constraining one covariate's effect at a time treats those tests (as though they are independent) doesn't tell you about the omnibus test with 100% certainty because those individual tests are correlated.  Correlated effects can lead to seemingly counter-intuitive results, like suppression effects, that are perfectly valid.

So I don't have specific advice about what to do.  If no individual covariate's effect shows strong evidence of differing across groups, then I suppose constraining them all across groups is justified even if that omnibus test is significant (maybe it's a Type I error?).  And maybe that means a subsequent test of equality of latent-intercept means would not be biased enough by the possibly invalid constraint to cause concern.  If you decide to report that test, I would recommend addressing that uncertainty as a limitation in your Discussion section.
Does this then indicate the presence of a 3-way interaction?
No, it doesn't sound like it. See above for where to look for a 3-way interaction between Time, Group, and a covariate.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

parts:
For future research, would you propose to test the maximal model immediately (including all (time-variant and time-invariant) predictors) or build up from smaller models (which I now did)?
Testing the full model first might give a more complete representation.
I am interested what your thoughts are on this.

SEMNET would be a good place to post this general SEM question

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

But I agree with your intuition.  In OLS or multilevel regression framework, one can add predictors sequentially to test effects of one set after controlling for another.  But in SEM, you cannot compare the fit of models to different (subsets of) data, so you are probably better off entering the entire set of covariates at once to test their effects.  But it is perfectly reasonable to first build your LGCM without any covariates, to assess assumptions of linearity, variability in random effects, etc.  Then add the covariates to see what predicts the random effects (i.e., latent intercept and slope) -- but recall you cannot compare the fit of that model to the fit of a model that does not include covariates at all.

On Monday, October 9, 2017 at 9:37:36 AM UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
but this is not the effect that I am looking for (?) (i.e. whether there is an overall difference in slope), since I am interested in the difference of the slope between groups.

What about the slope?  The average slope?  The syntax that constraints the slope (co)variances to zero posits that individuals (within both groups) have identical trajectories.  If you want to compare the average slope across groups, you need to constrain that parameter to equality

s ~ c(a1, a1)*1


1. Is there a way of constraining the slopes per group with the growth() function?
(do I use 'group =' or not?)

If you want to compare groups, you need the group= argument.  Are you asking about the group.equal= argument?  Specifying group.equal = "means" would constrain all latent means to equality across groups, which is not what you want.  Use the syntax I showed above.

3. Is this approach also applicable when investigating the full model including the predictors?

If you have predictors of the slope, then you are comparing intercepts across groups.  Thus, the test would be conditional on how your predictors are centered.  This is the same as the homogeneity of slopes assumption when comparing "adjusted means" in ANCOVA (equivalent to comparing intercepts).  To make an unconditional test of equality of intercepts, the effects of predictors on the latent growth factors would have to be constrained to equality across groups.  You should test that set of constraints first, to make sure it holds.  If it does not, then that implies an interaction between the predictor(s) and the Randomization variable.  In which case you could probe the interaction by centering the predictors at 2 or 3 meaningful values, and testing equivalence of intercepts at each of those values.

http://quantpsy.org/interact/lca2.htm

Kaloyan,
I am coming into this conversation late and may have missed something.  However, I think perhaps it was not clear to you what the '1' in c(a1,a1)*1 represents.  This is not the fixed effect of the slope on the second time point.  Instead, it is part of the syntax for specifying an intercept, which is the effect of a constant set to 1.  See the mean structures page in the online lavaan tutorial and the model.syntax help file section #4.  It seems to me that you want to test the equality of the mean of the slope across groups: s ~ c(a1,a1)*1 versus s ~ c(a1,a2)*1.  For example, if the estimates were 1 and 2 for the two groups, then that would predict mean growth of 0,1,2,3 in the first group and 0,2,4,6 in the second group.  Note that there is nothing special about the labels 'a1' and 'a2' they could be 'intGroup1' and 'intGroup2', 'a' and 'b', or 'Ben' and 'Jerry'.  The chi-square difference test between models using the above to specifications will provide a test of equality and you can also define a difference score as a defined parameter to obtain a confidence interval.

In your output for each group, you should see estimates for the intercept of the slope that look something like this.

Intercepts:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)

.s       (a1)    0.975    0.042   23.475    0.000

Keith
